Title: Stepping down from the Design Team

Messages.Author: Amenophobis
Messages.Body:
Dear V:EKN Inner Circle:

With a certain amount of sadness, we are submitting this jointly written letter. Although our time working on the V:EKN Design Team has been, on the whole, meaningful and productive, for quite a while now we have become less and less satisfied with the situation. The loss of direction of the project, some team members with whom we work, and the new targets and the methods of accomplishing goals make it increasingly difficult for us to feel our contributions are appreciated. This concern has been especially highlighted by recent communications with some members of the Inner Circle. Despite our repeated attempts to establish common ground, it has become clear that there are insurmountable differences between most of the Inner Circle and the remaining Design Team on one side and us on the other.

As a consequence, we are resigning from the V:EKN Design Team, effective immediately. This decision was not taken lightly and we believe this is the best solution for all parties involved.

The rest of the Inner Circle seems to have complete confidence in the Design Team Leader. Therefore, we are removing ourselves and our cards, so that the Design Team Leader has ample opportunity to develop his own creative ideas.

The cards we have designed are not to be used by the V:EKN Design Team. Since the creative content for Round 1 originated from our work (including Jeff Kuta’s), and had no significant contributions from the remaining Design Team members, we insist that the Design Team refrains from further playtest of such cards and from including them in the upcoming set without our explicit permission. This creative content includes all of the cards from Round 1, with one exception, and any other ideas that we initiated and explored.

At this time, the V:EKN does have permission to continue work on the six storyline reward cards. We also want to respect and acknowledge the creative efforts of the volunteer artists, so special consideration may likely be given to the handful of cards with already commissioned artwork.

We are only resigning from the Design Team. Carl intends to continue his responsibilities as Austrian National Coordinator. Eric plans to stay as the Inner Circle Storyline Coordinator, especially to help shepherd the storyline reward cards through the remainder of the process.

We both are committed to continuing to serve the V:TES player base.

Sincerely,

Carl Pilhatsch and Eric Chiang

pckvtes.wordpress.com

Messages.Author: Amenophobis
Messages.Body:
Dear V:TES Community,

We are aware of the concerns that have been expressed so far and want to reassure the players it was never our intent to withhold our cards from the community. We apologize if we were not clear enough about what we are intending to do.

Eric, Jeff, and I are going to continue developing our cards on our own and these cards will be freely available for use by the public. We will be doing this voluntarily out of our love for the game – we are not seeking to make any monetary profit.

When we are finished with our set after additional public playtesting (any players interested in playtesting would be welcome), we will make the set available to the public and the V:EKN has the option to sanction the use of our set in official V:EKN tournaments. We would be pleased if they did.

In the past, some players have specifically stated that they don’t care how the cards are designed, they just care about the end results. The fact that we are now working independently should not matter if it still results in quality cards. This could be beneficial to the V:TES community if it means that more quality cards are developed. More ideas means more potential expansions.

We will be finishing up our current Sabbat set and will be ready for Round 3 soon. We have already started work on our next set which will focus on the Laibon sect.

pckvtes.wordpress.com

> Joscha wrote:
> And for future sets we should appoint developers, who really want to work for the game and not for their egos.
>
Amen.

Look, creative people get differences in opinion. That's normal. But what needs to happen, a lot, is what's called "Killing Your Darlings": if testing reveals that your cherished creations do not work well in practice, you need to get rid of them. No matter how much you're in love with what you've created, and no matter how much you personally believe in them.

This sort of thing needs to be a group effort. I don't know the details of what's going on here (though I've heard some bits and pieces which I'll keep private via off-forum channels), but it's clear that it's a personality/ego issue.

All that matters in the end is the quality of the cards being designed, and whether or not they work in actual play. Period.

Messages.Author: jamesatzephyr
Messages.Body:
> Shard wrote:

If it was not a HttB rare, I feel we would see more decks with more copies of it in the TWDA. It was printed as a rare for a reason.
>
This is totally bogus card design.

V:TES absolutely, positively knew when it was created that rarity simply cannot balance a card. Magic had shown that players would buy thousands upon thousands of cards if they liked the game enough, when Garfield's initial design for it assumed people would probably pick up maybe a few hundred cards - and that a complete set would either not happen or be very rare.

As a result, V:TES has pretty much never used rarity as a balancing factor. Many of the more niche cards tend towards rare/uncommon (or vampire, in sets that support that rarity), and staple cards towards common. Certainly, mistakes have been made, and I'm sure that some choices have been made with an eye towards, you know, making a profit and all that. But many massively powerful cards are common - Govern the Unaligned is still, pound for pound, pretty much one of the most powerful cards in the game and has been in something like 9 different sets, both as a normal card and as a fixed card in pre-cons. Super easy to get.

If a card is too powerful, the correct response is not to make it rare because *someone* will collect them all on Ebay and then fuck up a Continental Championship with it. (Or, if you prefer, Jyhad Online.) The correct response is to make the card a more balanced card.

Messages.Author: jamesatzephyr
Messages.Body:
> Shard wrote:
> Cavalier is arguably the best Archetype in the game. I do not understand how you all think a permanent inferior freak drive is not great.
>
That's because you're changing your argument. No-one is saying it is not potentially very cool, or useful to a variety of decks. It's not a total no-brainer - it competes for master card space; some decks already have good untap potential; not every deck is necessarily succeeding at enough actions (bruise-and-X decks that get blocked a lot? not the strongest archetype, but certainly played); and not every deck that would like more untap has masses of spare blood and/or is using actions that cost blood.

But it's totally not a bad card. It's up there with Perfectionist, sure, which is also arguably a top tier archetype.

It was not made rare in order to prevent lots of players getting access to lots of copies because the game would break if that happened. If the card was very overpowered or broken, that can't be addressed by rarity.

Personally, were there the option to in the relevant sets, I'd have made most of the (playable) archetypes uncommon. (And not printed the rubbish ones, obviously.) Or possibly vampire rarity - which works out to much the same thing, roughly. The earlier ones are probably too common. But when you basically only have common or rare to pick from, then these things happen.
